pr_title: Performance Issue #3622 Log handling via a dedicated thread
pr_body:
<!--- Provide a general summary of your changes in the Title above -->

#### Description
<!--- Describe your changes in detail -->
The current implementation of log handling has thread contention over which thread is using the logger. The new baseloghandler class implements a queue log system that allows the rest of the engine to post log messages to a logging queue and then alert the logging thread that there is new messages that need to be processed. Then the logging thread can process each message in the queue through the implementing classes log methods. 

This PR does change the functionality of the console and file log handlers to implement the new abstract BaseLogHandler class; now the console and file log handlers contain a set of methods for writing to their respective outs (WriteDebug, WriteTrace, WriteError) which is called on by the Logger Thread.

#### Related Issue
<!--- This project only accepts pull requests related to open issues -->
<!--- If suggesting a new feature or change, please discuss it in an issue first -->
<!--- If fixing a bug, there should be an issue describing it with steps to reproduce -->
<!--- Please link to the issue here: -->
Closes #3622 

#### Motivation and Context
<!--- Why is this change required? What problem does it solve? -->
- Performance improvement since it removes thread contention for logger
- Separates i/o functions from the rest of the worker and engine threads which is a safer approach.

#### Requires Documentation Change
<!--- Please indicate if these changes will require updates to documentation, and if so, specify what changes are required -->
None

#### How Has This Been Tested?
<!--- Please describe in detail how you tested your changes. -->
<!--- Include details of your testing environment, and the tests you ran to -->
<!--- see how your change affects other areas of the code, etc. -->
Unit test included TestLoggingSpeeds(int x); these are ignored by default.
x = number of threads writing to the log. Each thread writes 1000 messages concurrently to the log. 

Comparing the current implementation vs this new one shows pretty significant differences, cuts the time to about half.

pr_comments:
What is the behavior during fatal runtime errors? These log files are the singular source for determining why a live algorithm unexpectedly fails. If these messages are backed in a queue then it's possible they never get written to disk before the process terminates. This is potentially exacerbated by the fact that the thread is initialized as a background thread which means the CLR will exit the process with that thread still running. We may want to test add some tests to provide confidence around such failure modes.

Also, when running locally it's incredibly useful that the console logs are synchronously ordered and relate to current processing events. With this change, we break this temporal coupling and the console logs are now a view of delayed processing. The value of this is left to the reader to decide.

> Also, when running locally it's incredibly useful that the console logs are synchronously ordered and relate to current processing events. With this change, we break this temporal coupling and the console logs are now a view of delayed processing. The value of this is left to the reader to decide.

Yeah, I've been thinking of this too, we could add a `Log` config bool flag, e.g `Log.AsynchronousEnabled`, so we can disable this feature _if_ we have some explosion so solve. The `BaseLogHandler` could check this config value on `Error/Debug/Trace` and enqueue or directly push the log.
Note that the order of the logging is still respected here and the time will match the enqueue time too.

We will close this for now as `WillNoFix` since the benefit for Lean logging usage does not overcome the problems associated with runtime explosions and the potential loss of those precious last logs.

issue_context.title: Consolidate logging to reduce thread contention on single log file
issue_context.body:
<!--- This template provides sections for bugs and features. Please delete any irrelevant sections before submitting -->

#### Expected Behavior
<!--- Required. Describe the behavior you expect to see for your case. -->
Log spamming shouldn't block threads.

#### Actual Behavior
<!--- Required. Describe the actual behavior for your case. -->
Log spamming causes lots of thread contention as threads wait for their turn to write _and flush_ to a single log file.

#### Potential Solution
<!--- Optional. Describe any potential solutions and/or thoughts as to what may be causing the difference between expected and actual behavior. -->
Queue up log messages and have a separate thread be responsible for writing them. We should also consolidate the messages to provide for less write operations in total.

#### Reproducing the Problem
<!--- Required for Bugs. Describe how to reproduce the problem. This can be via a failing unit test or a simplified algorithm that reliably demonstrates this issue.  -->
Run and algorithm lots of sparse data sets and observe the slower than expected run time due to log file contention from missing data log spam.

review_comments:
This may need to be marked as `volatile` now since it's being read from a background thread but its value could be changed from a foreground thread which makes the read in `WriteMessage` potentially stale.

Another option is to change it to a `CancellationTokenSource` which manages the thread memory barriers correctly and efficiently.
Should always use `UtcNow` -- it sucks when you run a test and you just happen to cross over daylight savings time :)

I have a sneaking suspicion that we've introduced a potential race by removing the synchronization on dispose. While it's incredibly unlikely (even impossible in this code base) for multiple threads to call dispose at the same time, it's arguably negligible on performance to leave it in. Locked objects that are not in contention are pretty cheap to acquire, especially when the acquire count is once (one app exit)
I think in places of the code we re-route the console, so this may not be safe unless we first grab the reference in a static constructor and save it (`Console.Out`)
True! I think we could actually directly call `WriteError` here, `ConsoleLogHandler` and `FileLogHandler` will work correctly, file handler is disposing after the base
catch should be on a new line
